reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Results from reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, producing a painful vesicular rash respecting the midline
Hutchinson sign, vesicles at the tip or side of the nose (nasociliary nerve involvement), predicts a higher likelihood of ocular complications

Ocular manifestations are wide-ranging and include conjunctivitis, epithelial pseudodendrites, stromal and disciform keratitis, uveitis, scleritis, raised intraocular pressure, and, less commonly, retinitis and optic neuritis
Corneal sensation is frequently reduced, predisposing to neurotrophic keratopathy and persistent epithelial defects
Prompt systemic antiviral therapy, ideally started early in the rash, reduces the severity and frequency of ocular complications
Zoster pseudodendrites are raised mucous plaques without true end-bulbs, distinguishing them from the ulcerated dendrites of herpes simplex
Post-herpetic neuralgia is a common and debilitating sequela, and zoster in a young or immunocompromised patient should prompt evaluation for underlying immunosuppression
reference.pathophysiology: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus residing in the trigeminal ganglion after childhood chickenpox. Declining cell-mediated immunity, with age or immunosuppression, allows the virus to travel down the ophthalmic division, causing a dermatomal vesicular eruption and neuritis. Direct viral cytopathic effect, immune-mediated inflammation, and an occlusive vasculitis of ocular vessels together produce the diverse anterior and posterior segment complications. Sensory nerve damage leads to reduced corneal sensation, neurotrophic keratopathy, and chronic neuropathic pain (post-herpetic neuralgia).
additionalDifferentials: Contact or allergic dermatitis of the periocular skin
Other causes of acute anterior uveitis or keratitis
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to identify keratitis, pseudodendrites, uveitis, and scleritis
Intraocular pressure measurement, as secondary pressure rise is common
Dilated fundus examination to exclude retinitis or optic nerve involvement
Evaluation for immunosuppression (including HIV) in young or atypical patients
Viral PCR of a lesion or ocular sample in uncertain cases
redFlags: Hutchinson sign indicating high risk of sight-threatening ocular involvement
Acute retinal necrosis or optic neuritis causing rapid visual loss
Neurotrophic keratopathy with a non-healing epithelial defect risking perforation
Zoster in a young or immunocompromised patient requiring evaluation of immune status
Signs of orbital or intracranial extension
reference.prognosis: Early antiviral treatment improves outcomes, but ocular involvement can become chronic and relapsing, with neurotrophic keratopathy, uveitis, glaucoma, and post-herpetic neuralgia causing long-term morbidity and potential visual loss.
pitfalls: Delaying antiviral therapy and increasing the risk and severity of ocular complications
Failing to examine the eye in a patient with a periocular zoster rash
Mistaking zoster pseudodendrites for herpes simplex dendrites
Overlooking reduced corneal sensation and evolving neurotrophic disease
Not screening for underlying immunosuppression in young patients
management: Start systemic antiviral therapy with aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir as early as possible in the rash to reduce the severity and frequency of ocular complications

Manage ocular inflammation with topical corticosteroids for keratitis and uveitis under specialist supervision, cycloplegics for comfort, and pressure-lowering agents for secondary ocular hypertension
Protect the neurotrophic cornea with intensive lubrication and, where needed, lid-closure procedures for persistent epithelial defects
Treat post-herpetic neuralgia with neuropathic agents such as tricyclic antidepressants or gabapentinoids, and provide skin care for the dermatomal rash
Evaluate for underlying immunosuppression including HIV in young or atypical patients, and advise zoster vaccination as prevention in eligible individuals
Refer to ophthalmology with dilated fundus examination to exclude retinitis and optic neuritis, escalating for posterior segment or sight-threatening disease
